newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Yields rise in subdued Australian bond market.
newsitem.headline: Yields rise in subdued Australian bond market.

text.p: *Australian bond yields rose slightly in early trading in anticipation of a large rise in today's release of housing finance data for April at 11.30 a.m. (0130 GMT).
*Market chews over RBA's PAR requirements changes.

Australian bond yields rose slightly during a slow start to the session, partly reflecting the softer close in U.S. Treasuries, and in anticipation of a large rise in today's release of housing finance data.

The April data at 11.30 a.m. (0130 GMT) is expected to show a hefty rise of 12.0 percent after the 1.3 percent fall in March with analysts pointing to private data showing commitments from the major banks rose some 15.0 percent in the period.
However, "This data is not what the Reserve Bank is looking at, so it shouldn't have much impact. The key will be tomorrow's jobs figures," one trader said.
The market also remained pre-occupied by the Reserve Bank's alterations to the prime asset ratios (PAR) that commercial banks are required to hold, announced on Tuesday.
The bank is cutting PAR to three percent from six percent as of June 23 and is now allowing the inclusion of semi-government bonds in the requirements.

Semis had rallied initially on the announcement, although such a move had been rumoured for sometime, and its impact was slightly watered down by the overall PAR reduction to three percent. However, the wider issue is what impact the increased liquidity will have on the market, traders said.

"There is no reason to dive in and buy semis now as they are already tightly priced to government bonds. The extra liquidity is going to have a bigger impact at the short end as banks, I assume, would have had their holdings in the cheapest stocks," one trader said.

Analysts at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell believe there should be some outright selling of bonds and semis because the banks are no longer the captive holders they once were. They said that latest statistics showed that banks held A$21.8 billion of government stocks in March, so hypothetically a full three percentage point drop would free up A$9.7 billion of PAR stock.

The softer tone saw the market give up some of Tuesday's narrowing trend to the dollar bloc. This was particularly notable at the long-end against Canada, which was boosted by foreign buying and spread narrowing trades to the U.S.. The 30-year U.S./Canada spread is now trading around parity.
